title: India Exempt From $20,000 US Visa Bond Rule as 50 Countries Listed
excerpt: The US State Department has finalized a permanent visa-bond program for B1/B2 applicants from 50 countries, with bonds of $10,000 to $20,000 set at consular officers' discretion. Indian passport holders are not on the list.
body:
• India is not on the list. Indian passport holders are exempt from the US visa-bond requirement; 50 countries are covered, including Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal in South Asia.
  • Who pays and how much: B1/B2 (business/tourist) visa applicants from listed countries may be asked by a consular officer to post a bond of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 — the amount is set during the visa interview, and not every applicant will be asked.
  • Payment mechanics: The bond is posted only after a consular officer directs it, via Form I-352 through Pay.gov. Money paid without an officer's instruction is not refunded — a warning that matters for scam prevention.
  • The list can grow. The State Department says countries can be added on 15 days' public notice, so today's exemption is not a guarantee.

The United States has finalized a permanent visa-bond program that can require applicants from 50 designated countries to deposit up to $20,000 before receiving a B-1 business or B-2 tourist visa. The program, made permanent through a final rule that took effect on August 3, 2026, leaves India off the list — meaning Indian passport holders face no bond obligation under the current framework.

The rule replaces a one-year pilot program run in 2025 with the Departments of State, Homeland Security and the Treasury. The pilot offered three bond tiers — $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000. The final version drops the $5,000 floor entirely and adds a $20,000 ceiling, restructuring the tiers to $10,000, $15,000 and $20,000. The exact amount an applicant pays is fixed by the consular officer during the visa interview, and paying a bond does not guarantee visa approval.

The full country list

The program applies to nationals of 50 countries whose passports determine coverage — applying from a different country does not remove the requirement. About 30 of the 50 are African states. The Asian countries on the list are Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Georgia, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mongolia, Nepal, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. The remaining entries cover the Caribbean (Antigua and Barbuda, Cuba, Dominica, Grenada), the Pacific (Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu) and Latin America (Nicaragua, Venezuela).

Implementation rolled out in phases: Malawi and Zambia have been covered since August 20, 2025; The Gambia since October 11, 2025; Mauritania, São Tomé and Príncipe and Tanzania since October 23, 2025; Bhutan, Botswana, the Central African Republic, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Namibia and Turkmenistan since January 1, 2026; a large group including Bangladesh, Nepal, Nigeria, Cuba and Venezuela since January 21, 2026; and Cambodia, Ethiopia, Georgia, Grenada, Lesotho, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Nicaragua, Papua New Guinea, Seychelles and Tunisia since April 2, 2026.

How the bond works

The authority comes from Section 221(g)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which empowers consular staff to require a bond as a condition of visa issuance. Critically, consular officers retain discretion: not every applicant from a listed country will be asked to post a bond, and the amount is set case by case within the $10,000–$20,000 range.

"Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers."

— Federal Register notice finalizing the visa bond rule

Applicants must wait for the officer's instruction before submitting DHS Form I-352. After that, they receive a direct payment link for Pay.gov, the Treasury Department's digital payment system, and accept the bond terms through that platform. The State Department warns that payments made without official instructions will not be refunded, and says the US government takes no responsibility for money transferred outside its systems.

A friend, family member or business associate can pay the bond on an applicant's behalf; the payer's name must match the name recorded on Form I-352, and any refund goes to the person who paid. Payments and refunds are both in US dollars, with the payer bearing any exchange-rate losses. Bondholders must enter and leave the United States through commercial airports — charter flights, private aviation, land crossings and sea routes are prohibited. Refunds depend on following visa and bond conditions; the notice describes automatic refunds in several situations, including qualifying departures and unused visas. Overstaying, late extension requests and certain protection applications can count as breaches and trigger review.

Impact and analysis

The State Department justifies the program as an overstay-reduction measure, citing B1/B2 overstay statistics from the Department of Homeland Security's Entry/Exit Overstay Report and concluding from the 2025 pilot that bonds are an effective compliance tool. Immigration advocates counter that requiring thousands of dollars upfront could discourage legitimate business and tourist travel to the United States — a criticism that will likely follow the program as it becomes permanent.

For Indian travelers, the immediate picture is straightforward: no bond applies. But the structure of the program gives consular officers broad discretion, and the State Department has explicitly said the country list may expand. The removals can take effect immediately, while additions require at least 15 days' public notice on Travel.State.Gov.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian-American community, which frequently hosts relatives from South Asia, the list's coverage of Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal matters in practice: a cousin traveling on a Bangladeshi or Nepali passport faces the bond requirement even if the host family in the US is Indian. Coverage turns on nationality and the passport used, so dual nationals and families across borders should check which document they will travel on.

What's next

Watch the State Department's visa bond country page on Travel.State.Gov — it was last updated on May 13, 2026, and any expansion of the roster will appear there at least 15 days before taking effect. For now, Indian passport holders can apply for B1/B2 visas under the same process as before, while applicants from the 50 listed countries should prepare for the possibility of a bond demand at their interview.
